15. Main Menu @COMMENT_BODY@ Career Creation

When players first launch the game, they should encounter a polished main menu.

Main menu options:

- Play.
- Start Career.
- New Save Slot.
- Load Career.
- Settings.

Players can create multiple independent career saves.

Character Creation

Before beginning a career, players choose:

- First name.
- Last name.
- Stage name.
- Birth date.
- Starting year.
- Starting location.
- Character appearance.

Real names and stage names should be independent.

After creating their character, players enter the main simulation and can customize their appearance whenever they want.

16. Character Customization @COMMENT_BODY@ Fashion

Character customization must remain accessible throughout the entire career.

Players can change:

- Skin tone.
- Hairstyles.
- Facial features.
- Clothing.
- Jewelry.
- Tattoos.
- Accessories.

Fashion Freedom

Fashion must NOT be restricted to the current historical decade.

Players can freely combine:

- Modern fashion.
- Vintage fashion.
- 1970s clothing.
- 1980s clothing.
- 1990s clothing.
- 2000s fashion.
- Contemporary streetwear.
- Luxury designer fashion.

Historical availability should affect the shopping catalog, not restrict the player's personal style.

Clothing Shopping

Create a dedicated CLOTHING tab.

Players can:

- Browse clothing categories.
- Purchase individual items.
- Build outfits.
- Save favorite outfits.
- Change clothing at any time.
- Access previously purchased clothing permanently.

Include shirts, jackets, trousers, shoes, hats, coats, and complete outfits.

17. Main Gameplay Interface

The main gameplay screen should feature a clean, modern interface.

Main Dashboard

At the top:

- Character name.
- Stage name.
- Current age.
- Current year.
- Current week.
- Energy.
- Heat.
- Cash.
- Net worth.

Main Character Display

Show the player's customized character prominently.

Allow players to access customization directly from their character.

Career Overview

Display:

- Current career status.
- Popularity.
- Latest releases.
- Chart positions.
- Career milestones.
- Upcoming opportunities.

Music Industry News Feed

Underneath the character and career overview, display a continuously updating music industry news feed.

Example headlines:

- Legendary R@COMMENT_BODY@B singer announces retirement.
- Rising hip-hop artist signs a major record deal.
- Superstar releases highly anticipated album.
- Two artists engage in a public rivalry.
- Independent artist reaches Billboard Hot 100.
- Record label announces massive expansion.

Headlines should reflect actual events occurring inside the simulation.

18. Navigation Tabs

Introduce a permanent navigation system with dedicated sections.

MUSIC

- Create Songs.
- Singles.
- Albums.
- EPs.
- Discography.
- Collaborations.
- Groups.
- Producers.
- Recording Studio.

BUSINESS

- Record Labels.
- Artist Management.
- Signing Artists.
- Contracts.
- Label Finances.
- Investments.
- Business Opportunities.

CHARTS

- Billboard Hot 100.
- Billboard 200.
- Genre Charts.
- Artist Rankings.
- Global Charts.
- Certification History.

INDUSTRY

- Music Industry News.
- Artists.
- Relationships.
- Rivalries.
- Awards.
- Industry Events.

CLOTHING

- Clothing Store.
- Jewelry.
- Watches.
- Accessories.
- Tattoos.
- Outfit Customization.

LIFESTYLE

- Real Estate.
- Automotives.
- Garage.
- Property Portfolio.
- Luxury Purchases.

CHARACTER

- Appearance.
- Biography.
- Relationships.
- Career Statistics.
- Achievements.
- Net Worth.

19. Dynamic Music Charts

Charts must operate independently of the player.

Every week:

- Songs gain or lose popularity.
- New releases enter the charts.
- Older songs gradually decline.
- Viral songs can unexpectedly rise.
- Successful songs remain charting for multiple weeks.
- Artists compete against each other.
- Chart positions influence Heat and career opportunities.

BUILD A MUSIC INDUSTRY LIFE SIMULATOR — VERSION 1

Build a fully playable, interactive music industry life simulator inspired by BitLife, with deeper music mechanics, historical progression, artist management, character customization, and an open-ended lifestyle simulation.


The game should feel like a living music industry spanning the 1970s through the modern internet era. The player should be able to become a legendary musician, establish a record label, sign artists, form musical groups, accumulate wealth, develop rivalries, and build a lasting musical legacy.


IMPORTANT: This must be a functional game, not merely a static interface or a collection of mock buttons. All major gameplay systems should work, interact, and save their progress.


1. MAIN MENU & SAVE SYSTEM


When the player opens the game, display a polished main menu featuring:


- Play.
- Start Career.
- New Save Slot.
- Load Career.
- Settings.


Allow multiple independent career save slots.


Each save must preserve its own character, finances, discography, relationships, businesses, vehicles, properties, and progression.


2. CHARACTER CREATION


When starting a new career, allow the player to choose:


- First name.
- Last name.
- Stage name.
- Birth date.
- Starting year.
- Starting location.
- Initial character appearance.


The player should have both a real name and an artist name.


After character creation, the player enters the main dashboard.


Character customization must remain available throughout the entire career.


3. HISTORICAL PROGRESSION


The player begins their career in a chosen historical year, with the 1970s as the earliest starting era.


Progress through:


- 1970s.
- 1980s.
- 1990s.
- 2000s.
- 2010s.
- 2020s.
- Future decades where appropriate.


Every decade introduces historically appropriate:


- Music trends.
- Technology.
- Recording equipment.
- Distribution methods.
- Industry developments.
- Vehicles.
- Fashion collections.
- Artists.
- Cultural events.


The internet should emerge naturally during the appropriate historical period, followed by digital downloads, streaming, social media, and modern music promotion.


The music industry must evolve as time advances.


4. REAL ARTISTS & PROCEDURAL ARTISTS


Include recognizable real-world musicians from different historical generations.


Artists must appear during appropriate eras and develop naturally over time.


For example:


- 1970s soul and funk artists.
- 1980s R&B, soul, and New Jack Swing artists.
- 1990s R&B and hip-hop artists.
- 2000s contemporary R&B and hip-hop artists.
- 2010s and modern artists.


Artists should:


- Age naturally.
- Release music independently.
- Sign record deals.
- Collaborate with other musicians.
- Form groups.
- Experience career success or decline.
- Retire.
- Eventually pass away.


When artists retire or disappear, introduce procedurally generated musicians called REGens.


REGens should possess unique:


- Names.
- Stage names.
- Ages.
- Genres.
- Personalities.
- Careers.
- Discographies.
- Popularity.
- Relationships.
- Rivalries.


The industry must never become empty.


Real artists and fictional artists should coexist.


5. MUSIC CREATION SYSTEM


Music must be the central gameplay mechanic.


Allow players to create:


- Songs.
- Singles.
- EPs.
- Albums.
- Extended projects.
- Deluxe albums.
- Compilation albums.
- Group albums.


Every release should contain configurable attributes such as:


- Song title.
- Genre.
- Producer.
- Featured artist.
- Release date.
- Recording quality.
- Promotion.
- Production budget.


Genres should include:


- R&B.
- Soul.
- New Jack Swing.
- Hip-Hop.
- Rap.
- Funk.
- Disco.
- Pop.
- Neo-Soul.
- Contemporary R&B.
- Alternative R&B.
- Gospel.
- Rock.
- Jazz.


Players should be able to collaborate with artists, producers, and songwriters.


Songs should generate sales, streams, popularity, chart positions, and royalties over time.


6. DYNAMIC BILLBOARD & MUSIC CHARTS


Implement functioning music charts.


Include:


- Billboard Hot 100.
- Billboard 200.
- Genre-specific charts.
- Artist rankings.
- Global charts where appropriate.


Charts must contain numerous competing artists, not just the player.


Every simulated week:


- New releases enter charts.
- Songs rise or fall.
- Older songs gradually decline.
- Viral songs can unexpectedly rise.
- Successful songs can remain charting for multiple weeks.
- Artists compete for positions.
- Popularity and promotional activities influence chart performance.


The player should be able to achieve:


- Top 100 entries.
- Top 10 entries.
- Number One singles.
- Number One albums.
- Gold certifications.
- Platinum certifications.
- Multi-Platinum certifications.
- Diamond certifications.


Chart positions should influence Heat, popularity, record deals, and career opportunities.


7. HEAT SYSTEM


Introduce a dynamic mechanic called HEAT.


Heat represents the player's popularity, commercial momentum, cultural influence, and industry relevance.


Higher Heat should:


- Attract better record deals.
- Increase contract offers.
- Unlock major collaborations.
- Improve concert bookings.
- Increase media attention.
- Improve industry recognition.
- Increase demand for performances.


Heat should rise and fall based on releases, chart success, promotions, performances, controversies, and career activity.


Inactive musicians should gradually lose Heat.


8. RECORD LABEL & BUSINESS SYSTEM


Allow players to establish their own record labels.


Label management should include:


- Label name.
- Label logo.
- Signing artists.
- Artist contracts.
- Recording budgets.
- Release schedules.
- Label finances.
- Royalties.
- Promotion.
- Staff.
- Producers.
- Songwriters.
- Artist management.
- Label expansion.


Artists signed to the player's label should have independent careers.


They should release songs, gain popularity, generate revenue, and develop their own relationships and rivalries.


Allow players to receive offers from existing record labels.


Players should be able to negotiate:


- Signing bonuses.
- Advances.
- Royalties.
- Contract duration.
- Creative control.
- Ownership rights.


The player must be able to become an independent artist, a signed artist, or a record label owner.


9. ARTIST RELATIONSHIPS & RIVALRIES


Every artist should have an evolving relationship system.


Relationship categories:


- Acquaintance.
- Friend.
- Close Friend.
- Collaborator.
- Mentor.
- Rival.
- Enemy.
- Industry Associate.


Allow players to:


- Meet artists.
- Develop friendships.
- Collaborate.
- Feature artists on songs.
- Produce music for other artists.
- Start rivalries.
- Respond to criticism.
- Compete for chart positions.
- Resolve rivalries.
- Maintain long-term competitive relationships.


Artists should also independently initiate relationships and rivalries.


Rivalries should influence news coverage, popularity, collaborations, fan reactions, and career opportunities.


10. GROUPS & BANDS


Allow players to create musical groups.


Players should be able to:


- Recruit members.
- Form duos.
- Create bands.
- Establish supergroups.
- Select group names.
- Manage group members.
- Release group singles.
- Release group albums.
- Share royalties.
- Experience creative disagreements.
- Break up.
- Reunite.


Members can be real historical artists or procedurally generated musicians, provided the timeline is appropriate.


Groups should have independent popularity, discographies, and careers.


11. CHARACTER CUSTOMIZATION & CLOTHING


Character customization must be extensive and accessible at any time.


Allow customization of:


- Skin tone.
- Hairstyles.
- Facial features.
- Clothing.
- Jewelry.
- Watches.
- Accessories.
- Tattoos.


The player must be able to purchase clothing and permanently retain purchased items.


Clothing categories include:


- Shirts.
- Jackets.
- Trousers.
- Shoes.
- Hats.
- Coats.
- Complete outfits.
- Luxury fashion.
- Streetwear.
- Vintage fashion.


Fashion must NOT be restricted to the current decade.


A player in the 1970s can wear modern-inspired clothing.


A player in the 2000s can wear 1990s-inspired clothing.


A player in 2026 can wear 1980s fashion.


Historical availability should influence the shopping catalog, but the player must retain complete freedom over their aesthetic.


Include a clothing store, outfit builder, saved outfits, and permanent wardrobe inventory.


12. JEWELRY & ACCESSORIES


Create a dedicated jewelry shopping system.


Allow purchases of:


- Chains.
- Necklaces.
- Rings.
- Watches.
- Bracelets.
- Earrings.
- Luxury accessories.


Jewelry should be permanently added to the player's collection.


Players should be able to equip, unequip, and combine accessories with outfits.


13. TATTOOS


Allow players to purchase tattoos and customize their character with them.


Include:


- Tattoo designs.
- Tattoo placement.
- Multiple tattoos.
- Tattoo collections.
- Optional tattoo removal.


Tattoos should remain part of the character unless removed.


14. AUTOMOTIVE SYSTEM


Create a dedicated automotive shopping tab.


Vehicles should be historically appropriate to their release years.


Include:


- Classic cars.
- Luxury sedans.
- Sports cars.
- SUVs.
- Supercars.
- Vintage vehicles.


Cars should become available during appropriate historical periods.


Vehicles purchased in earlier decades must remain permanently in the player's garage.


For example, a car purchased in 1992 remains owned in 2026.


Players should be able to:


- Purchase cars.
- View their garage.
- Collect vehicles.
- Sell vehicles.
- Maintain their collection.


Once a vehicle's historical availability period ends, it should no longer be available for new purchases, but existing owners retain theirs.


15. REAL ESTATE & LIFESTYLE


Create a dedicated Lifestyle section.


Include:


- Apartments.
- Houses.
- Mansions.
- Luxury estates.
- Recording studios.
- Commercial properties.


Players should be able to:


- Purchase properties.
- Own multiple properties.
- Sell properties.
- View property portfolios.
- Generate rental income where appropriate.


Properties should remain owned across decades unless sold.


16. FINANCIAL & NET WORTH SYSTEM


Implement a comprehensive financial system.


Track:


- Cash.
- Music royalties.
- Streaming revenue.
- Sales revenue.
- Touring revenue.
- Label revenue.
- Investments.
- Property ownership.
- Vehicle collections.
- Expenses.
- Taxes.
- Contracts.
- Net worth.


Net worth should reflect actual financial assets and liabilities rather than cash alone.


Allow players to become millionaires, multimillionaires, or billionaires through music and business.


17. MAIN DASHBOARD & INTERFACE


Create a modern, polished, interactive dashboard.


The main screen should prominently display the player's character.


At the top of the dashboard, show:


- Character name.
- Stage name.
- Age.
- Current year.
- Current week.
- Energy.
- Heat.
- Cash.
- Net worth.


Underneath the character, display:


- Career status.
- Current popularity.
- Latest releases.
- Chart positions.
- Achievements.
- Career milestones.
- Upcoming opportunities.


Below the career overview, display a continuously updating MUSIC INDUSTRY NEWS FEED.


The news feed should contain headlines about artists, record labels, chart movements, rivalries, awards, releases, industry developments, and historical events.


18. NAVIGATION TABS


Implement permanent navigation tabs.


MUSIC:


- Create Songs.
- Singles.
- Albums.
- EPs.
- Discography.
- Collaborations.
- Groups.
- Recording Studio.


BUSINESS:


- Record Labels.
- Artist Management.
- Sign Artists.
- Contracts.
- Label Finances.
- Investments.


CHARTS:


- Billboard Hot 100.
- Billboard 200.
- Genre Charts.
- Artist Rankings.
- Certifications.


INDUSTRY:


- News.
- Artists.
- Relationships.
- Rivalries.
- Awards.
- Events.


CLOTHING:


- Clothing Store.
- Jewelry.
- Watches.
- Accessories.
- Tattoos.
- Wardrobe.
- Outfit Customization.


LIFESTYLE:


- Real Estate.
- Automotives.
- Garage.
- Property Portfolio.
- Luxury Purchases.


CHARACTER:


- Appearance.
- Biography.
- Career Statistics.
- Relationships.
- Achievements.
- Net Worth.


19. ENERGY POINTS SYSTEM


Implement a weekly Energy Points system.


The player begins each week with 100 EP.


Activities consume energy.


Example costs:


- Create a Song: 10 EP.
- Record a Song: 10 EP.
- Promote a Release: 5 EP.
- Collaborate with an Artist: 10 EP.
- Attend an Industry Event: 5 EP.
- Perform a Concert: 15 EP.
- Business Activities: Variable EP.


Energy prevents players from completing unlimited activities in a single week.


Activities should have meaningful differences in cost and reward.


Energy should encourage strategic decisions without becoming unnecessarily restrictive.


20. NEXT WEEK SYSTEM


The main progression button should be NEXT WEEK.


When clicked, the game advances exactly one simulated week.


During weekly progression:


1. Process music releases.
2. Calculate streams and sales.
3. Update music charts.
4. Calculate royalties and revenue.
5. Update record label finances.
6. Update artist relationships.
7. Update rivalries.
8. Generate music industry headlines.
9. Process random events.
10. Update Heat.
11. Update popularity.
12. Calculate expenses and net worth.
13. Display a weekly financial and career report.
14. Restore Energy to 100 EP.


After the report, the player returns to the dashboard with a fresh week of activities.


21. WEEKLY REPORT SYSTEM


Every completed week should generate a detailed report.


Display:


- Streams gained.
- Sales generated.
- Chart movements.
- Certifications earned.
- Revenue received.
- Expenses paid.
- Net worth changes.
- Heat changes.
- Rivalry developments.
- Artist relationship updates.
- Industry headlines.
- Career opportunities.


Reports should be dynamic and reflect the player's actual activities.


22. MUSIC INDUSTRY NEWS SYSTEM


Create a dynamic news generator.


News categories include:


- Artist releases.
- Chart updates.
- Record deals.
- Artist signings.
- Rivalries.
- Collaborations.
- Group formations.
- Group breakups.
- Awards.
- Retirements.
- Deaths.
- Industry acquisitions.
- Label expansions.
- Unexpected commercial successes.


News should reflect actual simulated events.


Do not repeatedly display identical generic headlines.


23. RANDOM EVENTS & ANTI-REPETITION


The game must avoid repetitive gameplay.


Introduce a dynamic event system that creates unpredictable situations.


Possible events:


- A record label offers a contract.
- An artist requests a collaboration.
- A rival challenges the player.
- A song unexpectedly becomes popular.
- A group experiences creative disagreements.
- A producer offers a unique opportunity.
- A record label wants to sign one of the player's artists.
- A music award nomination arrives.
- A major artist announces retirement.
- An independent musician becomes a breakout star.


Events should provide meaningful choices and consequences.


The game should never rely solely on repetitive button clicking to increase statistics.


24. GAME DESIGN PRINCIPLES


The game must prioritize:


- Freedom.
- Historical immersion.
- Replayability.
- Meaningful progression.
- Dynamic industry behavior.
- Player creativity.
- Persistent ownership.
- Evolving relationships.
- Functional systems.


Players must never be forced into a specific genre, fashion aesthetic, business strategy, or career path.


The player should be able to focus on music, business, lifestyle, or a combination of all three.


25. TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS


Build a fully functional game with:


- Persistent save data.
- Multiple career slots.
- Working navigation.
- Functional shopping systems.
- Functional music creation.
- Working charts.
- Working finances.
- Working record labels.
- Working relationships.
- Working rivalries.
- Working weekly progression.
- Working Energy Points.
- Functional artist generation.
- Historical progression.
- Dynamic news.
- Realistic simulation logic.


Use a modular architecture so additional features can be introduced in future versions.


Prioritize a playable Version 1 rather than attempting to implement every possible feature superficially.


All buttons must perform their intended actions.


All purchases must affect player inventory and finances.


All releases must influence the music simulation.


All weekly events must update the game state.


All major progression must be saved.


FINAL GAME VISION


Create a living music industry simulation where a player can start as an unknown musician in the 1970s, build a career through the decades, become a legendary artist, establish a powerful record label, sign musicians, form groups, create rivalries, purchase luxury items, collect historical vehicles, own real estate, and accumulate generational wealth.


The game should feel like an actual music-industry life simulator, not a repetitive menu-based game.


The player should feel like they are living through decades of musical history while building their own unique legacy.


Build Version 1 with a polished interface, functional mechanics, and expandable architecture.

- Songs.

- Song title.

- Promotion.
- Production budget.

- R&B.

- New Jack Swing.
- Hip-Hop.
- Rap.
- Funk.
- Disco.
- Pop.
- Neo-Soul.
- Contemporary R&B.
- Alternative R&B.
- Gospel.

- Jazz.

- Billboard Hot 100.
- Billboard 200.
- Genre-specific charts.
- Artist rankings.
- Global charts where appropriate.

- New releases enter charts.
- Songs rise or fall.
- Older songs gradually decline.
- Viral songs can unexpectedly rise.
- Successful songs can remain charting for multiple weeks.
- Artists compete for positions.
- Popularity and promotional activities influence chart performance.


The player should be able to achieve:


- Top 100 entries.
- Top 10 entries.
- Number One singles.
- Number One albums.
- Gold certifications.
- Platinum certifications.
- Multi-Platinum certifications.
- Diamond certifications.


Chart positions should influence Heat, popularity, record deals, and career opportunities.

Introduce a dynamic mechanic called HEAT.


Heat represents the player's popularity, commercial momentum, cultural influence, and industry relevance.


Higher Heat should:


- Attract better record deals.
- Increase contract offers.
- Unlock major collaborations.
- Improve concert bookings.
- Increase media attention.
- Improve industry recognition.
- Increase demand for performances.


Heat should rise and fall based on releases, chart success, promotions, performances, controversies, and career activity.


Inactive musicians should gradually lose Heat.

Allow players to establish their own record labels.


Label management should include:


- Label name.
- Label logo.
- Signing artists.
- Artist contracts.
- Recording budgets.
- Release schedules.
- Label finances.
- Royalties.
- Promotion.
- Staff.
- Producers.
- Songwriters.
- Artist management.
- Label expansion.


Artists signed to the player's label should have independent careers.


They should release songs, gain popularity, generate revenue, and develop their own relationships and rivalries.


Allow players to receive offers from existing record labels.


Players should be able to negotiate:


- Signing bonuses.
- Advances.
- Royalties.
- Contract duration.
- Creative control.
- Ownership rights.


The player must be able to become an independent artist, a signed artist, or a record label owner.


9. ARTIST RELATIONSHIPS & RIVALRIES


Every artist should have an evolving relationship system.


Relationship categories:


- Acquaintance.
- Friend.
- Close Friend.
- Collaborator.
- Mentor.
- Rival.
- Enemy.
- Industry Associate.


Allow players to:


- Meet artists.
- Develop friendships.
- Collaborate.
- Feature artists on songs.
- Produce music for other artists.
- Start rivalries.
- Respond to criticism.
- Compete for chart positions.
- Resolve rivalries.
- Maintain long-term competitive relationships.


Artists should also independently initiate relationships and rivalries.


Rivalries should influence news coverage, popularity, collaborations, fan reactions, and career opportunities.

Allow players to create musical groups.


Players should be able to:


- Recruit members.
- Form duos.
- Create bands.
- Establish supergroups.
- Select group names.
- Manage group members.
- Release group singles.
- Release group albums.
- Share royalties.
- Experience creative disagreements.
- Break up.
- Reunite.


Members can be real historical artists or procedurally generated musicians, provided the timeline is appropriate.


Groups should have independent popularity, discographies, and careers.

Character customization must be extensive and accessible at any time.


Allow customization of:


- Skin tone.
- Hairstyles.
- Facial features.
- Clothing.
- Jewelry.
- Watches.
- Accessories.
- Tattoos.


The player must be able to purchase clothing and permanently retain purchased items.


Clothing categories include:


- Shirts.
- Jackets.
- Trousers.
- Shoes.
- Hats.
- Coats.
- Complete outfits.
- Luxury fashion.
- Streetwear.
- Vintage fashion.


Fashion must NOT be restricted to the current decade.


A player in the 1970s can wear modern-inspired clothing.


A player in the 2000s can wear 1990s-inspired clothing.


A player in 2026 can wear 1980s fashion.


Historical availability should influence the shopping catalog, but the player must retain complete freedom over their aesthetic.


Include a clothing store, outfit builder, saved outfits, and permanent wardrobe inventory.

Create a dedicated jewelry shopping system.


Allow purchases of:


- Chains.
- Necklaces.
- Rings.
- Watches.
- Bracelets.
- Earrings.
- Luxury accessories.


Jewelry should be permanently added to the player's collection.


Players should be able to equip, unequip, and combine accessories with outfits.


13. TATTOOS


Allow players to purchase tattoos and customize their character with them.


Include:


- Tattoo designs.
- Tattoo placement.
- Multiple tattoos.
- Tattoo collections.
- Optional tattoo removal.


Tattoos should remain part of the character unless removed.


14. AUTOMOTIVE SYSTEM


Create a dedicated automotive shopping tab.


Vehicles should be historically appropriate to their release years.


Include:


- Classic cars.
- Luxury sedans.
- Sports cars.
- SUVs.
- Supercars.
- Vintage vehicles.


Cars should become available during appropriate historical periods.


Vehicles purchased in earlier decades must remain permanently in the player's garage.


For example, a car purchased in 1992 remains owned in 2026.


Players should be able to:


- Purchase cars.
- View their garage.
- Collect vehicles.
- Sell vehicles.
- Maintain their collection.


Once a vehicle's historical availability period ends, it should no longer be available for new purchases, but existing owners retain theirs.

Create a dedicated Lifestyle section.


Include:


- Apartments.
- Houses.
- Mansions.
- Luxury estates.
- Recording studios.
- Commercial properties.


Players should be able to:


- Purchase properties.
- Own multiple properties.
- Sell properties.
- View property portfolios.
- Generate rental income where appropriate.


Properties should remain owned across decades unless sold.

Implement a comprehensive financial system.


Track:


- Cash.
- Music royalties.
- Streaming revenue.
- Sales revenue.
- Touring revenue.
- Label revenue.
- Investments.
- Property ownership.
- Vehicle collections.
- Expenses.
- Taxes.
- Contracts.
- Net worth.

Create a modern, polished, interactive dashboard.

At the top of the dashboard, show:


- Character name.
- Stage name.
- Age.
- Current year.
- Current week.
- Energy.
- Heat.
- Cash.
- Net worth.


Underneath the character, display:


- Career status.
- Current popularity.
- Latest releases.
- Chart positions.
- Achievements.
- Career milestones.
- Upcoming opportunities.


Below the career overview, display a continuously updating MUSIC INDUSTRY NEWS FEED.


The news feed should contain headlines about artists, record labels, chart movements, rivalries, awards, releases, industry developments, and historical events.

Implement permanent navigation tabs.


MUSIC:


- Create Songs.
- Singles.
- Albums.
- EPs.
- Discography.
- Collaborations.
- Groups.
- Recording Studio.


BUSINESS:


- Record Labels.
- Artist Management.
- Sign Artists.
- Contracts.
- Label Finances.
- Investments.


CHARTS:


- Billboard Hot 100.
- Billboard 200.
- Genre Charts.
- Artist Rankings.
- Certifications.


INDUSTRY:


- News.
- Artists.
- Relationships.
- Rivalries.
- Awards.
- Events.


CLOTHING:


- Clothing Store.
- Jewelry.
- Watches.
- Accessories.
- Tattoos.
- Wardrobe.
- Outfit Customization.


LIFESTYLE:


- Real Estate.
- Automotives.
- Garage.
- Property Portfolio.
- Luxury Purchases.


CHARACTER:


- Appearance.
- Biography.
- Career Statistics.
- Relationships.
- Achievements.
- Net Worth.

Implement a weekly Energy Points system.


The player begins each week with 100 EP.


Activities consume energy.


Example costs:


- Create a Song: 10 EP.
- Record a Song: 10 EP.
- Promote a Release: 5 EP.
- Collaborate with an Artist: 10 EP.
- Attend an Industry Event: 5 EP.
- Perform a Concert: 15 EP.
- Business Activities: Variable EP.


Energy prevents players from completing unlimited activities in a single week.


Activities should have meaningful differences in cost and reward.


Energy should encourage strategic decisions without becoming unnecessarily restrictive.


20. NEXT WEEK SYSTEM


The main progression button should be NEXT WEEK.


When clicked, the game advances exactly one simulated week.


During weekly progression:


1. Process music releases.
2. Calculate streams and sales.
3. Update music charts.
4. Calculate royalties and revenue.
5. Update record label finances.
6. Update artist relationships.
7. Update rivalries.
8. Generate music industry headlines.
9. Process random events.
10. Update Heat.
11. Update popularity.
12. Calculate expenses and net worth.
13. Display a weekly financial and career report.
14. Restore Energy to 100 EP.


After the report, the player returns to the dashboard with a fresh week of activities.

Every completed week should generate a detailed report.


Display:


- Streams gained.
- Sales generated.
- Chart movements.
- Certifications earned.
- Revenue received.
- Expenses paid.
- Net worth changes.
- Heat changes.
- Rivalry developments.
- Artist relationship updates.
- Industry headlines.
- Career opportunities.


Reports should be dynamic and reflect the player's actual activities.

Create a dynamic news generator.


News categories include:


- Artist releases.
- Chart updates.
- Record deals.
- Artist signings.
- Rivalries.
- Collaborations.
- Group formations.
- Group breakups.
- Awards.
- Retirements.
- Deaths.
- Industry acquisitions.
- Label expansions.
- Unexpected commercial successes.


News should reflect actual simulated events.


Do not repeatedly display identical generic headlines.

The game must avoid repetitive gameplay.


Introduce a dynamic event system that creates unpredictable situations.


Possible events:


- A record label offers a contract.
- An artist requests a collaboration.
- A rival challenges the player.
- A song unexpectedly becomes popular.
- A group experiences creative disagreements.
- A producer offers a unique opportunity.
- A record label wants to sign one of the player's artists.
- A music award nomination arrives.
- A major artist announces retirement.
- An independent musician becomes a breakout star.


Events should provide meaningful choices and consequences.


The game should never rely solely on repetitive button clicking to increase statistics.


24. GAME DESIGN PRINCIPLES


The game must prioritize:


- Freedom.
- Historical immersion.
- Replayability.
- Meaningful progression.
- Dynamic industry behavior.
- Player creativity.
- Persistent ownership.
- Evolving relationships.
- Functional systems.


Players must never be forced into a specific genre, fashion aesthetic, business strategy, or career path.


The player should be able to focus on music, business, lifestyle, or a combination of all three.


25. TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS


Build a fully functional game with:


- Persistent save data.
- Multiple career slots.
- Working navigation.
- Functional shopping systems.
- Functional music creation.
- Working charts.
- Working finances.
- Working record labels.
- Working relationships.
- Working rivalries.
- Working weekly progression.
- Working Energy Points.
- Functional artist generation.
- Historical progression.
- Dynamic news.
- Realistic simulation logic.

Prioritize a playable Version 1 rather than attempting to implement every possible feature superficially.


All buttons must perform their intended actions.


All purchases must affect player inventory and finances.


All releases must influence the music simulation.


All weekly events must update the game state.


All major progression must be saved.

Create a living music industry simulation where a player can start as an unknown musician in the 1970s, build a career through the decades, become a legendary artist, establish a powerful record label, sign musicians, form groups, create rivalries, purchase luxury items, collect historical vehicles, own real estate, and accumulate generational wealth.


The game should feel like an actual music-industry life simulator, not a repetitive menu-based game.


The player should feel like they are living through decades of musical history while building their own unique legacy.


Build Version 1 with a polished interface, functional mechanics, and expandable architecture.

- Expand the existing music-career simulator into a playable, modular Version 1 music-industry life sim spanning historical eras, with meaningful music, business, relationship, lifestyle, and weekly simulation systems.

<subagent sessionID="ses_e5eb86df2ffeNEohU28uGyRtHc" state="completed">
Inspected `/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/game.js` in full. It is a single-file, client-side career simulator: saves live in `localStorage`, the UI is rendered from template strings, and gameplay actions are dispatched by `handleAction(a, el)`.

### Existing mechanics and main functions

- **Career and saves:** `newCareer(data)` creates a save with cash, energy, heat, popularity, releases, assets, wardrobe, charts, and feed. `persist()` and `getSave()` manage saves; `savesModal()` and the `load-save` action switch between them.
- **Navigation and UI:** `render()` selects a page; `dashboard()`, `musicPage()`, `chartsPage()`, `businessPage()`, `industryPage()`, `clothingPage()`, `lifestylePage()`, and `characterPage()` build the sections. `modal()` and the modal-specific functions handle forms and dialogs.
- **Music and weekly simulation:** `releaseModal()` and `commitRelease()` create releases. `advance()` increments the week, restores energy, changes chart scores, generates news, and pays streaming earnings.
- **Actions:** `handleAction()` routes career creation/loading, releases, gigs, radio, collaborations, producer and manager bookings, promotion, networking, clothing purchases/equipping, property purchases, appearance changes, and settings toggles.
- **Presentation helpers:** `chartRows()`, `releases()`, `feedItems()`, `avatar()`, `money()`, and `age()` format game data.

### Focused additions that fit the current structure

For a simulator expansion, the lowest-risk approach is to add one or two new state fields in `newCareer()`, render them in the relevant existing page, and handle changes in `handleAction()` or `advance()`. Examples that build on existing mechanics:

- Add **once-per-week action limits or a weekly action budget** for gigs, radio, networking, and other repeatable activities.
- Make **management, producers, and promotion persistent choices** with clear effects on later releases or weekly earnings; currently they are mostly one-time purchases.
- Add a small **career milestone/progression track** driven by existing releases, popularity, and chart performance.
- Keep new mechanics compatible with old saves by providing defaults when reading fields that older saves do not have.

### Bugs and caveats to account for

- **Actions can be repeated indefinitely within a week.** In particular, `gig`, `radio`, and `connect` can repeatedly grant money or popularity/heat; `manager` and `promo` can also be bought repeatedly.
- **Release age is calculated incorrectly across year boundaries.** `advance()` resets `week` each year, but streaming duration uses `c.week - r.week + 1`; a release from the prior year can therefore get a negative duration and fall back to minimum streams. Releases do not store their release year.
- **Chart results are not actually calculated.** `chartRows()` filters player entries out of `c.charts` and builds player rows from releases, but `commitRelease()` leaves `rank` at `0`, so chart appearances and release ranks never become meaningful. Several chart-page stats and news items are hardcoded.
- **Net worth updates are inconsistent.** Some expenses reduce `c.net`, but release costs do not. Property purchases subtract cash and then add the full property price to `c.net`, overstating wealth if `net` represents total assets.
- **Settings are mostly cosmetic.** The toggle only changes a CSS class and is not saved or used; the autosave switch has no action handler.
- **`releaseModal(type)` is defined twice** (lines 37 and 46). The later definition replaces the earlier one; they appear identical, so this is redundant rather than an immediate behavior change.
- **`age(c)` is approximate** and derives age from a fixed 2000 reference with a floor, rather than calculating the age at the career’s current date.

I did not edit any files.
</subagent>

## Objective
- Expand the existing music-career simulator into a playable, modular Version 1 music-industry life sim spanning historical eras, with meaningful music, business, relationship, lifestyle, and weekly simulation systems.
- Prioritize functional gameplay and persistent progression over superficially implementing every requested feature.

## Requirements
- Preserve the existing polished browser-game foundation while adding multiple independent career saves, character creation/customization, decade progression from the 1970s, evolving music technology and trends, and a living artist ecosystem with real historical musicians and procedurally generated REGens.
- Implement configurable releases and competing charts; dynamic Heat; relationships and rivalries; player-owned labels and signed artists; groups; wardrobe, jewelry, tattoos, vehicles, real estate; detailed finances; weekly Energy Points, progression, reports, events, and persistent saves.
- Ensure purchases, releases, activities, events, and buttons update game state; retain player freedom in genre, aesthetic, and strategy.

## Decisions
- Retain the dependency-free HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and browser `localStorage` foundation.
- No clarifying questions; make reasonable assumptions and briefly note them when finished.

## Work State
### Completed
- Inspected `game.js`, `index.html`, and `styles.css`; mapped the current rendering, state, and action-handling structure.
- Identified existing issues: charts do not calculate player ranks; weekly streaming age breaks across year boundaries; repeatable actions lack meaningful energy limits; net-worth updates are inconsistent; release configuration and weekly reporting are limited.

### Active
- Implement the requested Version 1 expansion; no code changes have been made for these requirements yet.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Add era-aware industry data, backward-compatible save-state migration, and a functioning weekly simulation with chart ranks, finances, Energy Points, and a dynamic weekly report.
2. Add working label, artist-signing, group, relationship, and event systems.
3. Expand configurable music releases and lifestyle/asset inventories, then verify progression, purchases, saves, and responsive layouts.

## Relevant Files
- `game.js`: Existing game state, rendering, simulation, and interaction handlers.
- `index.html`: Browser game entry point and script loading.
- `styles.css`: Interface styling and responsive layouts.

## Important Context
- Current code uses `localStorage` key `encoreSaves`; core functions include `newCareer`, `persist`, `advance`, `commitRelease`, and `handleAction`.
- An attempted creation of `systems.js` failed because the tool input exceeded its limit; the file was not created and `index.html` was not changed.
- Existing project files were previously reported as untracked/uncommitted; preserve user work.

## Objective
- Expand Encore into a playable, modular music-career life sim spanning historical eras, with meaningful music, business, relationship, lifestyle, and weekly simulation systems.
- Prioritize functional gameplay and persistent progression over superficially implementing every requested feature.

## Requirements
- Preserve the dependency-free HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and browser `localStorage` foundation.
- Support independent career saves, character customization, era progression from the 1970s, evolving music culture, historical musicians and procedurally generated artists.
- Make releases, charts, Heat, relationships, labels, signed artists, groups, lifestyle assets, finances, weekly Energy Points, reports, events, and save progression functional.
- Preserve player freedom in genre, aesthetic, and strategy.

## Decisions
- Keep the existing browser-game foundation and add the new systems as a separate script.
- Make reasonable assumptions without asking clarifying questions.

## Work State
### Completed
- Added `v1.js` with era-based historical artist rosters and migration for existing saves.
- Added weekly simulation for release streams, income and expenses, energy restoration, chart ranks, artist movement, annual era transitions, and weekly reports.
- Added configurable release promotion budgets and strategies, plus label founding, artist signing, group formation, networking, rivalries, and event choices.
- Connected the new systems by loading `v1.js` after `game.js` in `index.html`.
- `node --check game.js && node --check v1.js` passed before the latest small migration edit; headless Chromium loaded the menu without an observed JavaScript failure.

### Active
- Validate the new systems in interactive gameplay and address any integration or balance issues.
- Continue closing gaps against the broader Version 1 scope, including lifestyle/asset depth and progression.

### Blocked
- (none)

1. Re-run JavaScript syntax checks after the latest migration change and exercise career creation, releases, weekly advancement, saves, and new business/social actions in a browser.
2. Fix any discovered issues and review remaining scope gaps before wrapping up.

## Relevant Files
- `v1.js`: New era, simulation, economy, chart, event, release, label, group, and relationship systems.
- `game.js`: Existing UI, state, actions, and `localStorage` save foundation.
- `index.html`: Loads the game and V1 systems scripts.
- `styles.css`: Existing game layout and responsive styling.

- The latest edit initialized era-appropriate historical charts for migrated saves; checks were not rerun after that edit.
